but because of all the small mornings

At the grave we did not say “goodbye.”

When we go to heaven,
I think the gates are made of morning,
not pearl, but the first light
after a long night of rain.
I think the streets are full of voices
we have missed for years,
calling our names without sorrow,
as if we had only stepped out
for a little while.

There will be no clocks,
no locked doors, no last goodbyes.
The table will be long and open,
and every chair will be filled.
We will know each other
by the kindness in our hands.
We will remember the world
not as a wound, but as a garden
we once helped to keep.

There will be music in the ordinary:
a kettle’s small hymn,
a door left open,
a field of wheat leaning into wind.
We will sit together under trees
whose leaves have never known winter,
and tell the old stories
until they turn to gold.

Maybe God will be the quiet
in the middle of all that singing,
the warmth in the bread,
the light on every face.
And when we laugh,
it will be the laugh of children
who have finally found their way home.

When we go to heaven,

already multiplied.

and rooms resigned to rest.

and laid a finger on the door

my shadow at my heel,
through kitchen dark and hallway hush,
through what the floors conceal.
It silvered every sleeping chair,
the clock’s forgotten face,

and every tree a listener

The moon went round the house all night,

At last it touched the morning air
and thinned to thread and bone.
I stood beside the waking glass
and watched it go alone.
The rooms grew ordinary again,
the walls resumed their weight,
but something in me circled still,
still keeping moonlit gate.
